nature-res-020.title: The race to fish: a season shrinks to one day
nature-res-020.text: In Alaskan halibut fishing, the race once squeezed the whole season into a single 24-hour dash. The race to fish is the scramble to catch as much as possible during a short open season. Under a total allowable catch, each boat competes to land fish before the quota runs out. That pushes owners toward overcapitalization, buying more boat than the fishery needs. Catch shares, such as {{ref:nature-res-018}}, are designed to end it. Fishers can then schedule trips as they like, boom-and-bust market cycles fade, and no one needs to fish in hazardous weather. The resource-economics text says ITQs later ended overcapitalization and spread the catch over time.

nature-res-257.title: Agriculture: feeding cities, reshaping the land
nature-res-257.text:
Farming covers 4.8 billion ha, about one-third of the Earth's land, and touches land and water more than any other economic sector. Agriculture is the cultivation of soil and the planting and harvesting of food and non-food crops, together with livestock production. Broader definitions also take in forestry and aquaculture, though horticulture and forestry are often left out in practice.

Its surpluses let people live in cities and let population grow far beyond what hunting and gathering could sustain. The cost shows up in {{ref:nature-res-107}}. Expansion drives deforestation and degrades carbon-rich ecosystems such as peatlands, and about 40% of agricultural land is seriously degraded. Livestock occupy 70% of that land, which is 30% of the planet's land surface. Intensive farming raised yields by substituting synthetic fertilizers and pesticides for labour, but it increased water pollution and often relied on subsidies.

Agriculture, forestry and land use contribute between 13% and 21% of global greenhouse gas emissions, so it is tied to {{ref:nature-hist-007}}. FAO estimates that farms must produce about 50% more food, feed and fibre by 2050 than in 2012, adding pressure on water, land and soil.

nature-res-261.title: Water pollution: when water can no longer do its job
nature-res-261.text:
A 2017 study said polluted water spread gastrointestinal diseases and parasitic infections and killed 1.8 million people. Water pollution is the contamination of water bodies, usually by human activity, in a way that harms how they can be used. The bodies include lakes, rivers, oceans, reservoirs and groundwater. Water counts as polluted when it can no longer serve a use such as drinking, or when its ability to support fish and other life has changed significantly.

The main contaminants are pathogens, organic compounds such as petroleum hydrocarbons, inorganic ones such as heavy metals, nitrates, phosphates and silt, pharmaceuticals, and solid waste and plastics. Point sources are single identifiable outlets such as sewage plants and factories. Nonpoint pollution is diffuse, the summed effect of small amounts from a large area, and agriculture is a major contributor. Nutrient pollution is a primary cause of eutrophication, where excess nitrogen or phosphorus stimulates algal growth.

This is an {{ref:nature-found-031}} at work. Regulation is only part of the answer; education, economic instruments, market forces and stricter enforcement are also needed.

nature-res-273.title: Urbanization: the shift from fields to cities
nature-res-273.text:
Global urban area more than doubled from 33 Mha in 1992 to 71 Mha in 2015, consuming 24 Mha of fertile cropland and 3.3 Mha of forest. Urbanization is the process by which settlements grow as more people live and work in cities, shifting population from rural to urban areas. It refers to the proportion of a national population living in urban areas, not the absolute number of urban dwellers. The rural-urban balance stayed near a fixed equilibrium until the British Agricultural and Industrial Revolutions broke it in the late 18th century.

Cities offer labour-market access, education, housing and lower commuting costs, but also stress, higher living costs and marginalization. Their footprint reaches nature. Impervious surfaces send untreated runoff to streams and coasts instead of groundwater, and roads and railways fragment habitats, which harms biodiversity.

Global urbanization averaged 56.2% in 2020, with very low urbanization in belts across central-eastern Africa and central-southeast Asia. Planned urbanization follows an advance plan, as in the garden city movement, while suburbanization shifts residential areas outward.

nature-res-264.title: Commodities: goods the market treats as interchangeable
nature-res-264.text:
A bushel of wheat is a bushel of wheat, whoever grew it. That is the idea of a commodity: an economic good, usually a resource, whose instances the market treats as equivalent regardless of who produced them. Economists call this fungibility. Most commodities are raw materials, agricultural or mining products such as iron ore, sugar, rice and wheat. Crude oil, corn and gold are popular ones.

Price is set by the whole market, and established physical commodities have actively traded spot and derivative markets. On an exchange the contract's underlying standard defines the commodity, not any quality of a particular producer's product. Wide availability means smaller profit margins and makes factors other than price, such as brand, matter less. Soft commodities are grown goods like wheat or rice; hard ones include gold, silver and oil; energy commodities include electricity, gas, coal and oil.

Commoditization is a spectrum. Even electricity can be differentiated by generation method where buyers can pay more for renewables, and some customers pay for sustainability or animal welfare, so organic, cage-free or Forest Stewardship Council labels separate otherwise commodity goods.

nature-res-268.title: Trade: why regions swap what they make
nature-res-268.text:
People were swapping goods 50,000 years ago: ostrich eggshell beads are the evidence, and obsidian networks followed 15,000 years ago. Trade is the exchange of something of value for something else of value, pre-agreed as a contract. Prehistoric people did it in a gift economy before currency.

Trade exists because of specialization and division of labour, as people concentrate on a small part of production and trade their output. Regions trade because they have a comparative advantage in some goods, including scarce natural resources found elsewhere. The 1944 Bretton Woods Agreement set up the IMF and the World Bank to regulate the international economy and prevent national trade barriers.

International trade has helped develop the world economy but, with agreements lowering tariffs, has sometimes harmed local-product markets in poorer countries. South Korea's export-oriented industrialization did much better than India's historically closed policy, though effective state institutions also mattered.

nature-res-258.title: Bioenergy: fuel from living matter
nature-res-258.text:
In low-income countries, wood, charcoal, residues or dung burned in open fires or inefficient stoves still cook many meals. This traditional biomass is one face of bioenergy: renewable energy obtained by using biomass as fuel, whether wood, energy crops, harvest residues or organic waste. The IPCC defines it as energy from any form of biomass, meaning organic material excluding fossilised matter, so coal is not biomass here.

Wood and wood residues are the largest biomass energy source today. The main waste feedstocks are wood, agricultural, municipal solid and manufacturing waste. Biomass is upgraded by thermal, chemical or biochemical routes; thermal options are torrefaction, pyrolysis and gasification. In the EU in 2023 bioenergy was about three-quarters of renewable heating and cooling and nearly one-fifth of all heating and cooling.

Its climate benefit is not guaranteed. Over its life cycle bioenergy can emit less or more greenhouse gas than the energy it replaces, depending on how feedstock is grown, harvested and transported. Energy crops can displace natural ecosystems, degrade soils and use water and synthetic fertilisers, and about one-third of wood for traditional tropical heating and cooking is harvested unsustainably.

nature-res-266.title: Privatization: moving enterprises from state to market
nature-res-266.text:
Privatization gained worldwide momentum in the 1980s under Margaret Thatcher in the UK and Ronald Reagan in the US. It most commonly means moving something from the public sector into the private sector, such as selling a state-owned enterprise to private investors. It can also mean deregulation of a heavily regulated private industry, or contracting out government functions like water supply, revenue collection or prison management.

Governments tend to privatize more when public debt is higher, and when they cannot fund investment needed for profitability. World Bank and Megginson research in the early 2000s found that privatization in competitive industries with well-informed consumers consistently improved efficiency. Outcomes vary by model, though, and it is hard to separate the effects from wider economic trends.

The argument is still open. Proponents expect lower prices, better quality and less corruption, but concede that market failures and {{ref:nature-econ-350}} may be problematic. Opponents hold that goods and services everyone needs should stay with government so all have access, and that natural monopolies are better run by the state.

nature-res-262.title: Thermal pollution: when temperature is the contaminant
nature-res-262.text: Not every pollutant is a substance. Thermal pollution is the degradation of water quality by human activity that raises or lowers a water body's ambient temperature. Temperature is one of the physical changes that, along with chemicals and pathogens, can degrade aquatic ecosystems. It belongs with the other forms of {{ref:nature-res-261}}.

nature-res-263.title: Controlling water pollution at the source
nature-res-263.text: Municipal wastewater can be treated in centralized plants, decentralized systems, nature-based solutions or septic tanks; waste stabilization ponds are a low-cost option. Treated industrial effluent may be reused or released to a sanitary sewer or surface water. Construction sediment is managed with erosion controls such as mulching and sediment controls such as basins and silt fences. Controlling urban runoff means slowing stormwater flow and cutting pollutant discharges. In the United States the 1972 Clean Water Act amendments set up the main framework for improving water quality in surface waters.

nature-res-265.title: Commodity super cycles: a decade of high prices
nature-res-265.text: A commodity super cycle is a period of about a decade when commodities as a whole trade above their long-term moving average. One usually follows large industrial or commercial change that demands more resources. There have been four in the last 120 years. The latest began in 2000 as China joined the WTO and was halted by the 2008 recession. A 1970s boom ended when foreign investment fled as extractive industries were nationalized. The cycles apply to {{ref:nature-res-264}} as a group, not to any single one.

nature-res-269.title: Free trade: no favors for home producers
nature-res-269.text: Free trade is a policy by which a government does not discriminate against imports or exports through tariffs or subsidies. It does not mean a country abandons all control and taxation of imports and exports. In 1992 the European Union lifted barriers to internal trade in goods and labour. The WTO's Doha round aimed to lower trade barriers with a focus on fairness for developing countries, and agricultural subsidies were the hardest issue to settle.

nature-res-270.title: Protectionism: shielding home industry from imports
nature-res-270.text: Protectionist policies were particularly prevalent in the 1930s, between the Great Depression and World War II. Protectionism is the policy of restraining and discouraging trade between states, often through tariffs and restrictive quotas. Mill argued that a country with monopoly pricing power could manipulate its terms of trade through tariffs, which was taken as evidence against a universal doctrine of free trade. His infant industry argument holds that government should protect young industries only as long as they need to reach full capacity, and many industrializing countries adopted it. Most economists reject protection for unemployment, national defence and self-sufficiency (autarky) arguments, and overwhelmingly reject the view that bilateral trade deficits are harmful in themselves.

nature-res-271.title: Trade sanctions: punishing a country by cutting trade
nature-res-271.text: Trade sanctions are restrictions imposed on a country to punish it for an action. The severest is an embargo, a blockade of all trade. Embargoes are usually temporary, yet the US embargo on Cuba has lasted over 60 years.

nature-res-259.title: First- and second-generation biofuels
nature-res-259.text: Biofuels are classed as first-generation, made from food crops on arable land, or second-generation, made from non-food biomass. First-generation fuels come from crops such as sugarcane and maize. Bioethanol is fermented from their sugars or starch and is widely used in the United States and Brazil. Biodiesel comes from oils such as rapeseed and is the most common biofuel in Europe. Second-generation or advanced biofuels use perennial energy crops and agricultural residues, grown as by-products of a main crop or on marginal land.

nature-res-260.title: Surface power density: how much land a watt needs
nature-res-260.text: Power sources differ in how much land they need. Surface power density is the power a generation source delivers per square metre of land, which fixes how much land a given supply needs. One estimate of lifecycle density is 0.30 W/m2 for biomass, 1 for wind, 3 for hydro and 5 for solar. Lifecycle density counts land used by supporting infrastructure, manufacturing, mining or harvesting, and decommissioning. Another estimate gives medians of 0.08 W/m2 for biomass, 0.14 hydro, 1.84 wind and 6.63 solar, none above 10 W/m2.

nature-res-267.title: Five ways to privatize
nature-res-267.text: Privatization takes several main forms. A share issue sells the enterprise's shares on the stock market. An asset sale divests to a strategic investor, usually by auction. Voucher privatization gives citizens vouchers for part ownership of a corporation, usually free or very cheap. Privatization from below is the start of new private businesses in formerly socialist countries, and a management buyout lets managers buy public shares. Some sales, like Chicago's 2008 75-year parking meter deal, are criticised as secured borrowing that lets politicians raise money without taxes or debt.

nature-res-272.title: Urban economics: why cities form where they do
nature-res-272.text: Why do cities grow where they do, and why do land prices vary so much across space? Urban economics is a branch of {{ref:nature-econ-134}} that studies urban spatial structure and the location of households and firms. Unlike most neoclassical economics it focuses on spatial relationships, and it is rooted in the location theories of von Thünen, Alonso, Christaller and Lösch. It also asks why some cities are large and others small, and what drives growth and decline. O'Sullivan divides it into six themes: market forces in city development, land use, urban transportation, urban problems, housing policy and local government expenditure. Most urban economics today is neoclassical and centred on experiences in the Global North.
